titleText.es: Está celoso porque todo el mundo está en el desván escuchando a Stephen Colbert.
titleText.en: He's jealous because everyone is up in the attic listening to Stephen Colbert.
titleText.noteEn: The official English title text adds “just” before “jealous”; the Spanish archive keeps the same attic-and-Colbert joke without that extra emphasis.

regions.labelEs: ESTA HUELGA DE GUIONISTAS ES UNA MIERDA. TÚ NO VES SERIES.

applications.explanationEn: Es supplies the present form of ser, while una mierda forms the fixed vulgar negative judgment.
Tú is stated for contrast even though ves already identifies informal singular “you”; no supplies the negation between them.
Por and accented qué are written as two words because they directly ask for a reason.

regions.labelEs: SÍ, PERO ES UNA MIERDA ESTAR EN CAMPAÑA ELECTORAL SIN LOS COMENTARIOS DE JON STEWART.

excludedUnits.rationale: Jon is an English given name, not a Spanish lexical word.
Stewart is a surname, not a Spanish lexical word.

applications.explanationEn: Es supplies the present form of ser, while una mierda forms the fixed vulgar negative judgment.
Estar stays in its dictionary form after the preceding judgment, while en campaña electoral names the active election-campaign state.

regions.labelEs: CIERTO. ACABÉ HARTÁNDOME HACE UN PAR DE SEMANAS.

applications.explanationEn: Acabé gives the completed past viewpoint, and hartándome supplies the -ando action that became the eventual result for the speaker.
Hace comes before the complete duration un par de semanas to place the earlier change that far back from the present.
Un par de supplies the small approximate quantity, and semanas is the plural time noun being counted.
Dejaste gives the completed past form for informal singular “you,” de is required by the pattern, and seguir stays in its unchanged dictionary form.

regions.labelEs: NO. SECUESTRÉ A JON STEWART PARA QUE ME HICIERA SUS ANÁLISIS.

excludedUnits.rationale: Jon is an English given name, not a Spanish lexical word.
Stewart is a surname, not a Spanish lexical word.

applications.explanationEn: A appears before the specific person directly affected by secuestré; the two name tokens remain excluded from the Spanish vocabulary cards.

applications.exampleEs: PARA QUE ME HICIERA SUS ANÁLISIS
applications.explanationEn: Para que introduces the intended result, me identifies its beneficiary, and hiciera is the special past form because the analysis was the purpose of another past action.
Qué carries a written accent because it directly asks for information, even as a one-word question.
Está gives the present state, and masculine singular encerrado describes the result of someone having been confined.

regions.labelEs: ¡JON, OBAMA VA PRIMERO EN IOWA! ¡HAZME UN COMENTARIO AGUDO E IRÓNICO SOBRE LA SITUACIÓN!

excludedUnits.rationale: Jon is an English given name, not a Spanish lexical word.
Obama is a surname, not a Spanish lexical word.
Iowa is an English place name retained unchanged, not Spanish vocabulary.

applications.explanationEn: Va matches the single person being ranked, and masculine singular primero states the current first-place position.
Haz is the irregular positive tú command of hacer; the attached me does not change which command form is used.
Me is attached to the end of the positive command haz and the result is written as the single word hazme.
The usual y becomes e because irónico begins with the vowel sound i.

regions.labelEs: POR FAVOR, DEJA QUE ME VAYA. TENGO FAMILIA.

applications.explanationEn: Por and favor work together as the fixed politeness expression rather than contributing their usual separate meanings.
Deja is the positive command for one person addressed informally.
Deja requests permission from the listener, que opens the allowed action, me identifies the speaker, and ordinary voy changes to the requested-action form vaya.
Tengo states the general fact of having family, so familia follows directly without un or una even though natural English normally supplies ‘a.’

cards.noteEn: A huelga is a collective refusal to work, usually used to press for changes in pay or working conditions.

cards.promptEs: huelga de guionistas · Jon Stewart y los comentarios políticos
cards.answerEn: The joke refers to the 2007–08 U.S. writers' strike interrupting scripted television, including topical political comedy.
cards.noteEn: Jon Stewart hosted The Daily Show, whose writers helped produce its satirical analysis of current campaigns. The comic makes Black Hat solve the missing-commentary problem by kidnapping Stewart; the title text moves rival host Stephen Colbert to the attic.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; links an item to its type
cards.noteEn: Spanish often uses de between an item and the noun that identifies its type. English often puts the type noun first instead: libro de historia becomes “history book.”
Guionista names someone who writes scripts for film, television, radio, or similar productions. The same ending is used for men and women; the article shows the gender when needed.

example.es: Las guionistas preparan una nueva serie.
example.en: The screenwriters are preparing a new series.

cards.promptEs: ser una mierda, para juzgar algo
cards.questionEn: How can vulgar informal Spanish say that something is awful or worthless?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of ser followed by una mierda.
cards.noteEn: This fixed vulgar judgment literally uses the noun mierda, “shit,” but the whole expression describes a person, thing, or situation as very bad. Change ser for the person and time; una mierda stays fixed.

cards.answerEn: awful; terrible (in ser una mierda, vulgar)
cards.noteEn: Mierda literally means “shit.” In the vulgar judgment ser una mierda, it describes something as very bad, worthless, or deeply unpleasant rather than naming a literal substance.

cards.questionEn: Why might Spanish say tú or yo when the verb already tells you who acts?
cards.answerEn: Say the subject pronoun to add emphasis, contrast, or clarity; otherwise Spanish often leaves it out.
cards.noteEn: A verb form such as eres already points to “you.” Adding tú can stress that particular person, especially in a contrast or a surprised question. The pronoun may appear after the verb.

cards.answerEn: you watch (informal singular, television or a show)
cards.noteEn: Ver normally means “to see,” but with television, films, or shows it often corresponds to English “watch.” Ves is the present form for one person addressed informally.

example.en: Do you watch that series on Mondays?

cards.noteEn: Serie has the same spelling pattern as English “series,” but Spanish uses series as the plural form.
Write the question form as two words, with an accent on qué. Write the usual answer word porque as one word without an accent.
cards.questionEn: How do you write “why” and “because” in Spanish?

example.es: ¿Por qué estudias español? Porque me gusta.
example.en: Why do you study Spanish? Because I like it.

cards.answerEn: to be (in a state or condition)
cards.noteEn: Estar is the unchanged dictionary form used for states, conditions, and locations. After another conjugated verb, estar itself remains unchanged.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that a candidate or political team is actively campaigning?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of estar followed by en campaña, optionally adding electoral.
cards.noteEn: Estar changes for the person and time, while en campaña names the active campaign period. Electoral makes the election meaning explicit; without it, the surrounding political context can do that work.

cards.answerEn: on; engaged in (as part of estar en campaña)
cards.noteEn: Spanish uses en between estar and campaña to describe being actively engaged in a campaign. Natural English often says “campaigning” or “on the campaign trail.”
Campaña can name an organized effort. With electoral or in a political setting, it means an election campaign.

example.en: The election campaign starts in April.

cards.noteEn: Electoral has one form for masculine and feminine singular nouns: proceso electoral and campaña electoral.
Comentarios can mean individual comments or ongoing spoken analysis and commentary about events.

example.es: Escuchamos sus comentarios sobre el partido.
example.en: We listened to her commentary on the match.

cards.answerEn: by; from (identifying the creator or source)
cards.noteEn: De can connect a work, statement, or piece of commentary to the person who created or supplied it. Natural English often uses “by” rather than literal “of.”

example.en: I read an article by Marta.

cards.noteEn: Used as a brief response, cierto confirms that the preceding point is correct. This differs from cierto before a noun, where it can mean “a certain.”
Acabé is a completed-past form for the speaker. Before an action ending in -ando or -iendo, acabar can describe the final, sometimes unintended result: acabé riendo means “I ended up laughing.”

example.en: I ended up accepting the proposal.

cards.promptEs: acabar seguido de una acción en -ando o -iendo
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone eventually ends up doing something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of acabar followed directly by the action in its -ando or -iendo form.
cards.noteEn: Only acabar changes for the person and time. The second action uses the ongoing form ending in -ando or -iendo, often called a gerund. This pattern gives the eventual result, which may be unintended: acabamos riendo means “we ended up laughing.”

example.en: We ended up talking all afternoon.

cards.answerEn: getting fed up; becoming tired of it (the speaker)
cards.noteEn: Hartarse means to become fed up. The -ando form presents that change as an ongoing action, and the attached me identifies the speaker.

example.en: I'm getting fed up with the noise.

cards.noteEn: Before a length of time, hace tells you how long ago something happened. It does not mean “does” in this use.

cards.questionEn: How do you say how long ago a past event happened?
cards.answerEn: Put hace before the length of time.
cards.noteEn: Spanish places hace before a duration: hace dos semanas means “two weeks ago.” The verb that describes the event itself is normally in a past form.

cards.questionEn: How do you say “a couple of” before a plural noun?
cards.answerEn: Use un par de, then the plural noun.
cards.noteEn: The literal idea is a pair, but conversational un par de often gives an approximate small quantity. The noun after de is plural: un par de días, un par de preguntas.

example.en: I have a couple of questions.

cards.noteEn: Un par de before a plural noun commonly means “a couple of,” often an approximate small quantity rather than an exact matched pair.

example.en: I need a couple of minutes.

cards.answerEn: of; or no separate English word, linking an amount to what it measures
cards.noteEn: After a quantity expression, de introduces the substance or thing being measured. English uses “of” in expressions such as a lot of or the amount of, but may leave de untranslated in others, such as un poco de agua, “a little water.”
In dejar de followed by an unchanged action verb, dejaste says that one person addressed informally stopped doing that activity.

cards.answerEn: Use a form of dejar, then de, then the action verb in its dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form of a verb is called the infinitive. It usually ends in -ar, -er, or -ir. Only dejar changes to show who acts and when; the final verb stays in its dictionary form. Keep de in this pattern: dejar alone usually means “to leave” or “to let,” while dejar de + action means to stop doing that action.
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone stops doing something?

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; links dejar to the activity being stopped
cards.noteEn: De is required between a form of dejar and the following action in the common pattern dejar de hacer algo, ‘to stop doing something.’

cards.answerEn: to follow; keep track of (events or news)
cards.noteEn: Seguir can mean to follow developing news, a campaign, a competition, or another continuing sequence of events—not only to move behind someone physically.

example.en: I follow the news every day.

cards.noteEn: A campaña is a coordinated series of actions toward a goal, such as an election, advertising, or fundraising campaign.

example.es: Organizan campañas para ayudar al barrio.
example.en: They organize campaigns to help the neighborhood.

cards.noteEn: Secuestré is the completed-past form for the speaker. Its written accent keeps the stress on the final syllable.

example.es: En la película, el villano secuestró al científico.
example.en: In the film, the villain kidnapped the scientist.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; marks a specific person as the object
cards.noteEn: Spanish generally places a before a specific person who receives a verb’s action. This “personal a” is not translated as a separate English word.

cards.promptEs: a + persona o expresión que se refiere a una persona
cards.questionEn: Why does Spanish sometimes put a before the person affected by an action?
cards.answerEn: Put a before a person—or a word such as alguien or nadie—when that person directly receives the action.
cards.noteEn: This a is called the personal a. It is common before a named or specific person, but person-denoting words such as alguien (“someone”) and nadie (“nobody”) also take it. English usually has no separate word for it. Before the masculine article el, a + el contracts to al.

cards.answerEn: so that (before que and a desired result)
cards.noteEn: Before que and a full event, para introduces the purpose of an action. Translate para que together as ‘so that’ or ‘in order that.’

example.es: Hablo despacio para que todos entiendan.
example.en: I speak slowly so that everyone understands.

cards.questionEn: How do you express a purpose when someone or something else carries out the desired result?
cards.answerEn: Use para que, then put the result verb in the special form used for a purpose that is not yet a fact.
cards.noteEn: That special form is called the subjunctive. It appears because the second action is intended or desired, not presented as an established fact. For example, ordinary ve becomes vea, and ordinary viene becomes venga. Use para plus an unchanged action verb instead when the same person performs both actions.

example.es: Dejo una nota para que Ana la vea.
example.en: I leave a note so that Ana sees it.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; completes para que, ‘so that’
cards.noteEn: Que completes the purpose connector para que before an event with its own person or thing carrying out the action.

example.es: Cierra la puerta para que no entre frío.
example.en: Close the door so that cold air does not come in.

cards.answerEn: he would do; he did (special past form after para que)
cards.noteEn: Hiciera is a special past form of hacer used when a past action states the purpose or desired result of another past action. Ordinary hizo changes to hiciera after a frame such as para que.

example.es: Le escribí para que hiciera una copia.
example.en: I wrote to him so that he would make a copy.

cards.noteEn: Sus can mean “his,” “her,” “their,” or formal “your.” It agrees with the plural things possessed, not with the owner; context tells you whose they are.

example.es: El jefe llamó a sus empleados.

cards.noteEn: Análisis keeps the same written form in singular and plural. A plural article or another plural word shows when more than one analysis is meant.

cards.answerEn: Write qué, cómo, cuándo, and similar words with an accent when they ask a question or add an exclamation.
cards.noteEn: This includes direct questions (¿Qué quieres?), questions inside another sentence (No sé qué quiere), and exclamations (¡Qué bonito!). Without the accent, these words usually connect parts of a sentence instead: el libro que quiero means “the book that I want.”
cards.questionEn: Why do words such as que, como, and cuando sometimes have a written accent?

cards.promptEs: estar + forma de acción completada que describe un estado
cards.questionEn: How do you describe the state something is in as the result of an action?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of estar followed by the action's completed form, with an ending that matches the thing being described.
cards.noteEn: The completed form, often ending in -ado or -ido, is also called a participle. Estar changes for who or what is in the state. The participle changes like a describing word: cerrado, cerrada, cerrados, or cerradas. This pattern focuses on the resulting state, not on who performed the action.
Encerrado describes the resulting state of a masculine singular person or thing after being confined or shut inside.

example.es: El perro está encerrado en el patio.
example.en: The dog is shut in the yard.

cards.noteEn: The written accent belongs on the first syllable: sótano.

example.es: Guardamos las cajas en el sótano.
example.en: We keep the boxes in the basement.

cards.answerEn: is; currently ranks (in ir primero, “to be leading”)
cards.noteEn: In a ranking, a form of ir followed by primero, segunda, and so on gives the current position. Va primero means that one person or team is in first place.

example.en: Our team is in first place.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone or a team is currently in first place?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of ir followed by primero or primera to match the person or team being ranked.
cards.noteEn: Ir changes for the person and time. Primero changes to primera for a feminine singular person or thing, and plural rankings use primeros or primeras. The expression states a current position, not physical movement.

example.en: Our team is in first place.

cards.noteEn: Primero can claim or state first position in an order or ranking. With a movement verb such as ir, it can describe the current leader: va primero means that a person or team is in first place.

example.es: Daniel va primero en la carrera.

cards.answerEn: make me; give me (informal singular command)
cards.noteEn: Haz is the irregular positive command of hacer for one person addressed informally. Me attaches to its end and identifies the speaker as the person receiving or benefiting from what is made.

cards.promptEs: orden afirmativa para tú: habla, come, escribe
cards.questionEn: How do you give one friend or familiar person a positive command?
cards.answerEn: Use the informal singular command form, often the same form used for “he” or “she” in the present.
cards.noteEn: For many regular verbs, -ar becomes -a and -er or -ir becomes -e: hablar becomes habla, comer becomes come, and escribir becomes escribe. Some common verbs are irregular or change their stem. Negative commands use a different form and are a separate pattern.

cards.promptEs: imperativo afirmativo de tú + pronombre al final
cards.answerEn: Attach it to the end of the command and write the result as one word.
cards.noteEn: A positive command tells someone to do something, rather than not to do it. With one informal listener, sienta + te becomes siéntate. A written accent may be added so the combined word keeps the original stress. In a negative command, the short word goes before the verb instead: no te sientes.
cards.questionEn: If a positive command includes a short word such as te (“yourself”) or lo (“it”), where does that word go?

cards.noteEn: Comentario can be a written or spoken comment, including a short observation about current events.
For a remark or analysis, agudo describes quick, penetrating intelligence. In other settings it can instead describe a high-pitched sound or a sharp point.

cards.answerEn: and (used instead of y before an i sound)
cards.noteEn: Spanish changes y to e before a following word that begins with the vowel sound i, which makes the two words easier to distinguish in speech.

cards.promptEs: e en lugar de y antes de un sonido i
cards.questionEn: Why does Spanish sometimes use e where you expect y for “and”?
cards.answerEn: Change y to e before a word that begins with the vowel sound i.
cards.noteEn: The change avoids placing two similar i sounds together: padres e hijos. It is based on sound, not merely spelling, so y normally remains before words beginning with the consonant-like sound in hie-, as in nieve y hielo.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; part of por favor (“please”)

cards.noteEn: Por favor makes a request more polite. It can appear before or after the request.
Deja is the positive command for one person addressed informally. Before que and another action, it asks that person to allow the action.

cards.promptEs: dejar que otra persona haga algo
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone lets or allows another person to do something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of dejar, then que, then put the allowed action in its special requested-action form; state the person when the context does not already make them clear.
cards.noteEn: That special form is called the subjunctive because the action is being allowed or requested, not stated as an established fact. For example, ordinary decide changes to decida, and ordinary busco changes to busque. The person can be explicit, as in deja que Ana decida, or understood from the action form and situation, as in deja que busque, “let me search.” Dejar changes for the person and time; que remains unchanged.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; links dejar to the allowed action
cards.noteEn: After a form of dejar meaning “let” or “allow,” que introduces the allowed action. The person doing that action may be stated after que or understood from the situation and the verb form.

cards.answerEn: me (the speaker as the person allowed to act)
cards.noteEn: In a request such as deja que me siente, me belongs with the following action and identifies the speaker. Natural English likewise uses “me” after “let.”

cards.answerEn: I leave; I go (special form after deja que)
cards.noteEn: After deja que, the ordinary first-person form voy changes to vaya because the action is being requested or allowed rather than stated as a fact.

example.es: Mi madre deja que vaya solo.
example.en: My mother lets me go alone.

cards.questionEn: How can Spanish state the general fact of having a possession or family relationship without using un or una?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of tener followed directly by the singular noun when the general fact of having it is what matters.
cards.noteEn: Common examples include tener coche, tener casa, and tener familia. Natural English usually supplies ‘a’ in ‘have a car/house/family.’ Spanish often adds un or una when counting, emphasizing one particular item, or describing it: tengo una casa pequeña.
